newsitem.title: CANADA: Northstar must prove itself to market - CEO.
newsitem.headline: Northstar must prove itself to market - CEO.

text.p: Northstar Energy Corp, which has had a rocky stock market ride since its merger with Morrison Petroleums, must win investors over to its strategy in the coming months or possibly face a suitor itself, Northstar chief executive John Hagg said on Tuesday.
"We certainly must be prepared, I think, for any eventuality," Hagg told reporters after Northstar's annual meeting.
"Now that we've got a little bit of negative market momementum existing out there, we're going to have to prove ourselves. The market's going to be sitting there and they're waiting for results."

Earlier this year, Northstar merged with Morrison in a friendly C$700-million deal, struck after Canadian 88 Energy Corp scrapped a hostile offer for Morrison amid controversy over alleged securities impropriety.

Hagg said on Tuesday he continued to be surprised at how well Northstar's and Morrison's Alberta oil and gas properties fit together. The merger doubled oil and gas reserves as well as undeveloped landholdings for the company.
But investors have not reacted positively to the deal and the company's stock has been hammered over the past few months.

Northstar's shares hit a high in Toronto of 17.25 in December as strong prouction and reserves growth led to strong financial results. The stock was trading at 15.50 in the days after the merger announcement and fell to as low as 11.65 in May. Northstar closed on Tuesday at 12.65.

Hagg said he believed the poor market performance was partially due to arbitragers, who held stock in Morrison after Canadian 88 launched its bid but were unable to sell their entire positions into a C$14.50-a-share buyback in March.
Several fund managers used the opportunity to sell back their shares at a profit as the stock traded in the C$13.25 range at the time, leaving many arbitragers holding Northstar stock, he said.
Production growth in the early stages of the merger process has also been below analyst expectations, Hagg said.

"We produced 41,000 (barrels of oil equivalent a day) in the first quarter. At the time of the merger we would have run cases that varied between 45,000 and 49,000 barrels for the year. Our current outlook at 45,000 is probably at the lower end of that range," he said.

Hagg disputed remarks by Canadian 88 chief executive Greg Noval, published in a Canadian 88 press release last month, saying Northstar faced a "strong possibility" of writing down the value of some acquired Morrison assets.

"That's absolute baloney," he said, adding that Northstar, after reviewing assets following the merger, booked a just portion of the gas reserves at the Racehorse Creek in the Alberta Foothills that were previously booked by Morrison.
Northstar also planned to drill another well there.
Racehorse Creek was not a major focus of the takeover, but could still turn out to harbor large reserves, Hagg said.
He said total production was projected to average 45,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day in 1997 and 53,000 in 1998. That would be up from 24,500 barrels of oil equivalent a day in 1996.
Cash flow was expected to be C$185 million or C$2.55 a share in 1997 and C$25 million or C$3.25 a share in 1998. Northstar rang up cash flow of C$105.1 million or C$2.60 a share last year.
